246.about: Splits law-making power between Parliament and the States through the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule. In an overlap, Union List beats Concurrent, and Concurrent beats State.

key.c: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
key.issue: The Bombay Prohibition Act banned possession and sale of liquor. Liquor importers said this also hit imports, a Union subject.
key.q: Is a State law invalid because it incidentally touches a Union List subject?
key.held: No. Courts look at the pith and substance (true nature) of the law. This law was in substance about intoxicating liquor (State List), so it was valid; an incidental effect on imports does not make it invalid.
key.exam: Doctrine of pith and substance (first applied by the Privy Council in Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee, 1947).

key.c: Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India
key.issue: States levied cesses on mining land. Mine-owners said the Union's MMDR Act (List I, Entry 54) covers the field and that the royalty they already pay is itself a tax.
key.q: Is royalty a tax, and can States tax mineral rights and mineral-bearing land?
key.held: Royalty is not a tax; it is a contractual payment to the owner. States have power under List II Entries 49 and 50 to tax mineral-bearing land and mineral rights; Parliament's Entry 54 power does not take this away unless a law expressly limits it. India Cement (1989) overruled. Justice B.V. Nagarathna dissented.
key.exam: Fiscal federalism: a big win for mineral-rich States (Mains GS-2 Centre-State relations).

248.about: Anything not in any List belongs to Parliament. Residuary power is with the Centre in India and Canada, with the States in the USA and Australia.

key.c: Union of India v. H.S. Dhillon
key.issue: The Wealth Tax Act was amended to include the value of agricultural land in a person's net wealth. Taxes on land are a State subject (List II Entry 49), and List I Entry 86 excludes agricultural land.
key.q: Can Parliament tax wealth that includes agricultural land, using its residuary power?
key.held: Yes. If a matter is not in List II or List III, Parliament may legislate under Art. 248 and Entry 97 even if List I does not name it. A tax on the total capital value of a person's assets is not a tax on land, so the levy was valid.
key.exam: Test for residuary power: first exclude Lists II and III; residuary power is wide, not a last resort.

21.about: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Available to citizens and foreigners. After the 44th Amendment (1978) it cannot be suspended even in an Emergency (with Art. 20). The Supreme Court has read dozens of rights into it: dignity, livelihood, privacy, speedy trial, legal aid, clean environment, health, shelter, and more.

key.c: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
key.issue: A communist leader was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.
key.q: Does “procedure established by law” mean any procedure Parliament enacts, or a fair one? Must Art. 21 be read with Art. 19?
key.held: Narrow reading: any procedure laid down by a valid law is enough, and Arts. 19 and 21 work separately. Later overruled.
key.exam: Start of the story: from “procedure established by law” (Japan) towards due process (USA).

key.c: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
key.issue: During the 1975 Emergency the enforcement of Art. 21 was suspended and people were detained without trial.
key.q: Can a detainee file habeas corpus when Art. 21 is suspended?
key.held: No (4:1). Justice H.R. Khanna dissented. Overruled in Puttaswamy (2017); the 44th Amendment made Arts. 20 and 21 non-suspendable.
key.exam: Darkest hour of the Court; Khanna's dissent is a favourite Mains quote.

key.c: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
key.issue: Her passport was impounded “in public interest” without giving reasons or a hearing.
key.q: Must the procedure that takes away liberty be fair, just and reasonable?
key.held: Yes. The procedure must be just, fair and reasonable, not arbitrary. Arts. 14, 19 and 21 are linked (the “golden triangle”); Gopalan's narrow view was rejected.
key.exam: Brought due process into Art. 21 in substance.

key.c: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar
key.issue: Thousands of undertrials in Bihar jails had spent longer in jail than the maximum sentence for their offence.
key.q: Is a speedy trial part of Art. 21?
key.held: Yes: speedy trial and free legal aid are part of Art. 21; undertrials were ordered released.
key.exam: First big PIL; linked to Art. 39A (legal aid).

key.c: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
key.issue: Challenge to the death penalty for murder.
key.q: Is the death penalty constitutional?
key.held: Valid, but only in the “rarest of rare” cases, with reasons. Justice P.N. Bhagwati dissented.
key.exam: Machhi Singh (1983) later set the guidelines.

key.c: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
key.issue: Pavement dwellers in Bombay were to be evicted.
key.q: Does the right to life include the right to livelihood?
key.held: Yes, livelihood is part of life; eviction is allowed only by a fair procedure (notice, hearing).
key.exam: Socio-economic rights read into Art. 21.

key.c: Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
key.issue: Capitation fees in private professional colleges.
key.q: Is education a fundamental right?
key.held: Every child has a right to free education up to 14 years (read with DPSP Art. 45).
key.exam: Led to the 86th Amendment (2002): Art. 21A.

key.c: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
key.issue: Gang-rape of social worker Bhanwari Devi; no law on sexual harassment at the workplace.
key.q: Can the Court fill the gap?
key.held: Laid down binding guidelines using Arts. 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 and the CEDAW convention.
key.exam: Replaced by the POSH Act, 2013.

key.c: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
key.issue: Custodial deaths and torture.
key.q: What safeguards apply at arrest and in custody?
key.held: 11 guidelines on arrest (identity of officers, arrest memo, informing a relative, medical check) and compensation for custodial violence.
key.exam: Now partly in the CrPC/BNSS.

key.c: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
key.issue: Challenge to Aadhaar raised a prior question: is privacy a fundamental right?
key.q: Is the right to privacy protected by the Constitution?
key.held: Yes: privacy is intrinsic to Art. 21 and Part III. Overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) on this point, and ADM Jabalpur. Limits must pass a three-part test: legality, legitimate aim, proportionality.
key.exam: Privacy PYQs; base for Navtej, Joseph Shine and the data-protection law.

key.c: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
key.issue: Sec. 377 IPC criminalised consensual same-sex relations.
key.q: Does Sec. 377 violate Arts. 14, 15, 19 and 21?
key.held: Decriminalised consensual adult same-sex acts. Overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013).
key.exam: Dignity, privacy and constitutional morality.

key.c: Common Cause v. Union of India
key.issue: Right of terminally ill patients to refuse life support.
key.q: Does Art. 21 include the right to die with dignity?
key.held: Yes: passive euthanasia and living wills allowed with safeguards (procedure simplified in 2023).
key.exam: Aruna Shanbaug (2011) had first allowed passive euthanasia.

key.c: M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India
key.issue: Power lines in Great Indian Bustard habitat versus solar energy needs.
key.q: Is there a right against the effects of climate change?
key.held: Recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Arts. 14 and 21.
key.exam: Latest expansion; useful for environment and GS-3 answers.

14.about: Every person (citizen, foreigner, company) gets equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws. It forbids class legislation but allows reasonable classification, and since 1974 it also strikes down arbitrary State action.

key.c: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
key.issue: Sec 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 let the State Government send any "cases" or "classes of cases" to special courts that used a shorter procedure.
key.q: Can the executive pick which individual cases get a harsher procedure, with no guiding policy?
key.held: No. The power was unguided and arbitrary, so Sec 5 (as far as it covered individual cases) was void under Art 14. Classification must rest on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the law's object (the twin test, restated in Budhan Choudhry, 1955). Chief Justice Patanjali Sastri dissented.
key.exam: Classic twin test; the idea behind the Prelims 2021 question on unguided discretion.

key.c: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
key.issue: A senior IAS officer (Chief Secretary) was moved to a newly created post he said was a demotion.
key.q: Is Art 14 only about classification, or does it also forbid arbitrary action?
key.held: Transfer upheld, but Justice Bhagwati's opinion gave the new doctrine: equality is the opposite of arbitrariness; an arbitrary act is unequal and violates Arts 14 and 16.
key.exam: From the classification test to the arbitrariness test; carried on in Maneka (1978) and Ajay Hasia (1981).

key.c: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
key.issue: A woman divorced by instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) challenged the practice.
key.q: Is instant triple talaq valid, and can a law be struck down only because it is arbitrary?
key.held: Triple talaq set aside. Justices Nariman and Lalit: it is manifestly arbitrary (marriage broken on a whim, no chance to reconcile), so Sec 2 of the 1937 Shariat Act, as far as it recognised it, violates Art 14. Justice Kurian Joseph: not part of Islam. CJI Khehar and Justice Nazeer dissented (personal law; asked Parliament to legislate).
key.exam: Manifest arbitrariness applies to laws too; followed by the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.

key.c: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
key.issue: The Madras Communal G.O. (1927) split seats in State medical and engineering colleges by religion and caste.
key.q: Can the State fix admissions by caste and religion, relying on DPSP Art 46?
key.held: No. The G.O. violated Art 29(2) (no denial of admission on religion, race, caste, language). DPSPs cannot override Fundamental Rights. Parliament replied with the 1st Amendment (15(4)).
key.exam: First court-versus-Parliament round; FR vs DPSP story (C-G-K-M, Ch 7).

key.c: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
key.issue: A Mysore order reserved about 68% of seats in engineering and medical colleges for backward classes, SCs and STs.
key.q: How far can reservation under 15(4) go?
key.held: Struck down. Reservation must be reasonable, generally below 50%; caste may be one factor but not the only test of backwardness.
key.exam: Origin of the 50% ceiling, later fixed for jobs in Indra Sawhney.

key.c: P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra
key.issue: States imposed quotas and admission control on private unaided professional colleges.
key.q: Can the State force its reservation policy on unaided institutions?
key.held: No. The State cannot impose quotas on unaided private institutions, minority or non-minority. Parliament replied within months with the 93rd Amendment (15(5)).
key.exam: Second strike-and-patch round.

key.c: Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India
key.issue: The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006 gave 27% OBC seats in IITs, IIMs and central universities.
key.q: Are the 93rd Amendment and the 2006 Act valid?
key.held: Both upheld (for State and aided institutions; private unaided left open), but the creamy layer must be excluded from OBC seats. Creamy layer does not apply to SCs/STs.
key.exam: 27% OBC in central institutions; creamy layer rule in education.

key.c: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
key.issue: The 103rd Amendment gave 10% EWS reservation but left out the poor among SCs, STs and OBCs.
key.q: Does an economic-only quota that excludes SC/ST/OBC and crosses 50% violate the basic structure?
key.held: Valid. Economic criteria alone can ground special provisions; excluding groups already covered is not discrimination; the 50% ceiling is not inflexible. CJI U.U. Lalit and Justice S. Ravindra Bhat dissented (the exclusion violates the equality code).
key.exam: Basic structure + 50% rule; EWS in Mains.

key.c: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal case)
key.issue: The V.P. Singh government's 1990 order gave 27% of Central jobs to OBCs (Mandal). The 1991 Narasimha Rao order added preference for the poorer OBCs and 10% for economically backward among others.
key.q: Is caste-based OBC reservation valid, and what are its limits?
key.held: 27% upheld, with limits: creamy layer excluded; total reservation not above 50% except in extraordinary situations; no reservation in promotions under 16(4) (existing ones for 5 more years; overruled Rangachari, 1962, on this); the 10% economic quota struck down; a permanent body to revise OBC lists (NCBC, 1993). Justices Thommen, Kuldip Singh and R.M. Sahai dissented.
key.exam: Base of all reservation law; Parliament replied with the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments.

key.c: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
key.issue: Challenge to the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments on promotions.
key.q: Do these Amendments violate the basic structure?
key.held: Valid, but only enabling. Before a promotion quota the State must show backwardness, inadequate representation (quantifiable data) and overall efficiency (Art 335); the 50% cap and creamy layer still apply.
key.exam: The three conditions for promotion quotas.

key.c: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta

key.q: Was Nagaraj right on data and creamy layer?
key.held: No referral. Nagaraj was wrong to require data on SC/ST backwardness (they are presumed backward), but data on inadequate representation and Art 335 remain. Creamy layer applies to SC/ST promotions.
key.exam: Promotion chain: 77th Am → Nagaraj → Jarnail Singh.

key.c: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh

19.about: Six freedoms for citizens only: speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession. Each can be limited only by a law on the grounds in 19(2) to 19(6). Suspended automatically in a National Emergency declared on war or external aggression (Art 358).
19.pyq: Mains 2013 (Sec 66A) · Mains 2014 (free speech, hate speech, films) · Mains 2022 (movement and residence not absolute) (handout)
clauses: Speech (a) · assemble peaceably and without arms (b) · associations, unions, co-operative societies (c) · move (d) · reside (e) · profession, trade, business (g). No (f) since 1978
Speech limits: sovereignty and integrity, security of State, friendly relations, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence
Assembly: sovereignty, public order · Association: sovereignty, public order, morality
Movement and residence: interests of the general public, protection of Scheduled Tribes
Profession: general public interest, professional qualifications, State monopoly in any trade
amend: 19(2) rewritten: added friendly relations, public order, incitement and the word "reasonable"; 19(6) allows State trade monopolies (after Romesh Thappar)
added sovereignty and integrity of India to 19(2), (3), (4)
deleted 19(1)(f) property; Art 358 now suspends Art 19 only for war or external aggression, not armed rebellion

key.c: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
key.issue: Madras banned the entry of Romesh Thappar's journal Cross Roads under a public-safety law.
key.q: Can speech be curbed for "public order" when 19(2) then allowed only threats to the security of the State?
key.held: Ban struck down. Free speech includes freedom of circulation; public order is wider than security of the State, the only ground then. Justice Fazl Ali dissented. With Brij Bhushan (1950), it led to the 1st Amendment.
key.exam: Why "public order" entered 19(2).

key.c: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar
key.issue: A party worker was charged with sedition (Sec 124A IPC) for a speech attacking the government.
key.q: Is sedition a valid restriction under 19(2)?
key.held: Upheld but read down: only words that incite violence or tend to public disorder are sedition; strong criticism of government is not. In 2022 (S.G. Vombatkere) the Court kept 124A in abeyance; the BNS, 2023 dropped it (Sec 152 now covers acts endangering sovereignty).
key.exam: Sedition debate in Mains.

key.c: S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram
key.issue: The Madras High Court revoked the CBFC certificate of the Tamil film Ore Oru Gramathile (on reservation), fearing protests.
key.q: Can a certified film be stopped because some groups threaten violence?
key.held: No. The danger must have a proximate and direct nexus with the expression, "like a spark in a powder keg", not be remote or conjectural. The State must protect lawful expression: no heckler's veto.
key.exam: Films and free speech; heckler's veto.

key.c: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
key.issue: Two young women were arrested in Palghar (2012) for a Facebook post after Bal Thackeray's death, under Sec 66A of the IT Act.
key.q: Is Sec 66A (punishing "grossly offensive" or "annoying" messages) valid?
key.held: 66A struck down in full: vague, overbroad, chilling effect; annoyance is not a 19(2) ground. Discussion and advocacy are protected; only incitement can be curbed. Sec 69A blocking was upheld.
key.exam: Online speech; vagueness doctrine.

key.c: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
key.issue: Internet and movement curbs in Jammu and Kashmir after August 2019.
key.q: Are indefinite internet shutdowns valid?
key.held: Speech and trade through the internet are protected by 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g). An indefinite shutdown is not allowed; orders must be published, proportionate and reviewed. Sec 144 CrPC cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression.
key.exam: Internet shutdowns; proportionality test.

key.c: Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh
key.issue: A UP minister made remarks about the victims of the Bulandshahr gang-rape (2016).
key.q: Can extra limits beyond 19(2) be placed on speech, for example on ministers? Do Arts 19 and 21 bind private persons?
key.held: The 19(2) grounds are exhaustive; no extra restrictions. A minister's statement is not vicariously the government's. Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced even against non-State actors. Justice B.V. Nagarathna partly dissented (an official statement can be attributed to the government; called for a code of conduct).
key.exam: Hate speech by public figures; horizontal effect of rights.

key.c: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds)
key.issue: The Electoral Bond Scheme, 2018 allowed anonymous donations to parties; the Finance Act, 2017 removed disclosure and the cap on company donations.
key.q: Does donor anonymity violate the voter's right to information?
key.held: Scheme and amendments struck down. The voter's right to information about party funding is part of 19(1)(a); anonymity fails proportionality. Unlimited company donations are manifestly arbitrary (Art 14). SBI ordered to give details to the ECI.
key.exam: Electoral reform and transparency.

20.about: Three shields for an accused (citizen, foreigner or company): no ex-post-facto criminal law, no double jeopardy, no compelled self-incrimination. Criminal law only, not civil, tax or preventive detention. After the 44th Amendment it cannot be suspended even in an Emergency.
clauses: No conviction except for an act that was an offence when done; no penalty greater than the law then in force (a law reducing punishment can apply)
No one prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence (court proceedings only, not departmental)
No accused shall be compelled to be a witness against himself (testimonial evidence only)
amend: Art 359 amended: enforcement of Arts 20 and 21 cannot be suspended in a National Emergency

key.c: State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad
key.issue: Accused persons were made to give specimen handwriting and thumb impressions during investigation.
key.q: Is this being "compelled to be a witness" against oneself?
key.held: No. "To be a witness" means imparting personal knowledge (testimony). Thumb impressions, signatures, handwriting samples and showing the body are not self-incrimination.
key.exam: Basis of the testimonial vs physical split (BIO).

key.c: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
key.issue: Narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping tests were done on accused persons without consent.
key.q: Do forced scientific tests violate Art 20(3) and Art 21?
key.held: Yes. Involuntary tests violate 20(3) and personal liberty and mental privacy under 21. With consent and safeguards they may be done; the results are not admissible, but facts discovered through them may be used.
key.exam: Narco tests; 20(3) read with 21.

21A.about: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14, in the manner the State may by law decide. Added by the 86th Amendment (2002); works through the RTE Act, 2009 (in force 1 April 2010). Available to all persons, and it is a positive right that needs a law.

key.c: Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India
key.issue: Private schools challenged the RTE Act, mainly the 25% entry-level seats for weaker and disadvantaged children (Sec 12(1)(c)).
key.q: Can the 25% quota be imposed on private unaided schools?
key.held: RTE valid. The 25% quota applies to government, aided and unaided non-minority schools, but not to unaided minority schools (Art 30). Justice K.S. Radhakrishnan dissented (would exempt all unaided schools).

key.c: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India
key.issue: Challenge to the 86th Amendment (21A) and the 93rd Amendment (15(5)), and to RTE's reach over minority schools.
key.q: Do these Amendments violate the basic structure? Does RTE bind minority schools?
key.held: Both Amendments valid. The RTE Act does not apply to minority schools, aided or unaided; the 2012 view on aided minority schools was overruled. In 2025 (Anjuman Ishaat-e-Taleem Trust) a 2-judge bench doubted this and asked for a larger bench.

22.about: Two shields. Ordinary arrest: told the grounds as soon as possible, a lawyer of choice, and production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours (journey time excluded). Preventive detention (detention without trial to stop a future act): no detention beyond 3 months unless an Advisory Board of High Court judges finds sufficient cause; grounds and a chance to represent must be given. The first shield does not cover enemy aliens or preventive detainees.

key.c: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
key.issue: A communist leader was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.
key.q: Is preventive detention valid, and must it also satisfy Arts. 19 and 21?
key.held: The Act was upheld except Sec. 14 (which barred disclosing the grounds to the court). Art. 22 was treated as a complete code for preventive detention, separate from Arts. 19 and 21. Justice Fazl Ali dissented. This separate-boxes view was later rejected (R.C. Cooper 1970, Maneka 1978).
key.exam: Start of the preventive-detention story; same case is the Art. 21 starting point.

key.c: A.K. Roy v. Union of India
key.issue: The National Security Act, 1980 was challenged. The 44th Amendment's Sec. 3 (2-month limit, stronger Advisory Boards) had never been brought into force.
key.q: Is the NSA valid, and can the Court force the government to bring the 44th Amendment change into force?
key.held: NSA upheld. The Court refused to issue mandamus: Parliament had left the date of commencement to the executive. It added safeguards (detenu to be told grounds, kept near home, may take a friend, not a lawyer, before the Board).
key.exam: Why Art. 22(4) still says 3 months: the 44th Amendment clause was never notified.

key.c: Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra
key.issue: A man was arrested in the Mumbai BMW hit-and-run case without being given written grounds of arrest.
key.q: Must the grounds of arrest be given in writing for every offence, or only under special laws like PMLA and UAPA?
key.held: Written grounds, in a language the arrested person understands, for every offence under every law (IPC/BNS included). If that is not possible at once, tell him orally and give the written grounds at least 2 hours before he is produced for remand. Non-compliance makes the arrest and remand illegal.
key.exam: Latest step in the Art. 22(1) chain: Pankaj Bansal 2023 → Purkayastha 2024 → Vihaan Kumar 2025 → Mihir Shah 2025.

25.about: Every person (citizen or foreigner) has freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health and the other Fundamental Rights. The State may still regulate the secular side of religion and make social-reform laws, including opening Hindu public temples to all Hindus.

key.c: Commissioner, HRE Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar (Shirur Mutt)
key.issue: The Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 gave officials wide control over a math (monastery) and its affairs.
key.q: How far can the State control a religious institution?
key.held: Religion covers rituals and observances, not only belief. Only the secular side (money, property, administration) can be regulated; essential religious practices are protected. Some sections of the Act were struck down.
key.exam: Origin of the Essential Religious Practices (ERP) test.

key.c: Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh
key.issue: MP and Orissa laws banned conversion by force, fraud or inducement.
key.q: Does the right to propagate include a right to convert others?
key.held: No. To propagate is to spread one's faith, not to convert another person; forced conversion hurts the other person's freedom of conscience. The State anti-conversion laws were upheld (public order).
key.exam: Base for today's State anti-conversion laws and the Mains debate on them.

key.c: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala)
key.issue: Women aged 10-50 were barred from the Sabarimala temple under a Kerala rule.
key.q: Is excluding women of menstruating age protected by Arts. 25 and 26?
key.held: The bar was struck down: devotees of Ayyappa are not a separate denomination and the exclusion is not an essential practice; it violates women's rights under Art. 25(1). Justice Indu Malhotra dissented. Review led to a 9-judge reference on Arts. 25-26 and ERP (heard April-May 2026; judgment reserved on 14 May 2026).
key.exam: Constitutional morality vs faith; watch for the 9-judge verdict.

29.about: Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture may conserve it, so it covers majorities too, not only minorities. No citizen can be denied admission to a State-run or State-aided educational institution only on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.

key.c: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
key.issue: Madras's Communal G.O. fixed medical and engineering college seats by religion and caste.
key.q: Can the State allot seats on caste and religion to carry out the Directive Principles?
key.held: No. The G.O. violated Art. 29(2) (and 15(1)). DPSPs cannot override Fundamental Rights.
key.exam: Led to the 1st Amendment (1951), which added Art. 15(4).

key.c: State of Bombay v. Bombay Education Society
key.issue: A Bombay order barred pupils whose mother tongue was not English from English-medium schools, hitting Anglo-Indian schools.
key.q: Who can claim Art. 29(2)?
key.held: The order was struck down. Art. 29(2) protects every citizen, majority or minority, and a minority school cannot be forced to turn students away by language.
key.exam: 29(2) is an individual right for all citizens; Art. 30 is for minorities only.

30.about: Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. The State cannot deny aid only because of minority management, and if it acquires their property, the compensation must not defeat the right (30(1A)). “Minority” is not defined; courts decide it State by State.

key.c: In re Kerala Education Bill, 1957
key.issue: The President asked whether the Kerala Education Bill's controls on aided schools (teacher appointment, fees) were valid against minority schools.
key.q: How far can the State regulate minority institutions that take aid?
key.held: Minorities may run institutions of their choice, including general (non-religious) education. The State may set reasonable conditions for aid and recognition, but not conditions that destroy the minority character. A minority is judged with reference to the State whose law is in question.
key.exam: First word on Art. 30: “regulate, but do not destroy”.

key.c: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
key.issue: Many cases on admissions, fees and State control over private and minority colleges.
key.q: How is a minority identified, and how much autonomy do minority and private institutions have?
key.held: Minority status (religious and linguistic) is decided State-wise, not nationally. The right to administer is not a right to maladminister: the State may regulate standards. Unaided institutions get wide freedom on admissions and fees (no capitation).
key.exam: Why Hindus can be a minority in Punjab, Mizoram, Nagaland etc.

key.c: P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra
key.issue: States imposed their quotas and admission rules on unaided professional colleges.
key.q: Can the State force reservation on unaided institutions, minority or not?
key.held: No. The State cannot impose its quota or admission policy on unaided institutions (Arts. 19(1)(g) and 30).
key.exam: Answered by the 93rd Amendment (2005): Art. 15(5) allows quotas in private institutions except minority institutions.

key.c: Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India
key.issue: The RTE Act's 25% weaker-section seats (Sec. 12(1)(c)) were applied to private and minority schools.
key.q: Do the 93rd Amendment and the RTE Act bind minority schools?
key.held: Art. 15(5) and Art. 21A are valid, but the RTE Act does not apply to minority schools, aided or unaided, since it would harm their Art. 30 rights.
key.exam: Mains: inclusion (21A) vs minority autonomy (30). A 2025 bench doubted Pramati and sought a larger bench.

key.c: Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal
key.issue: Is AMU a minority institution, though it was made a university by a 1920 Act of the legislature?
key.q: Does creation by a statute end minority status under Art. 30?
key.held: No. Statutory incorporation does not end minority character; the test is who established it (origin, purpose, community's role), and Art. 30 covers pre-1950 institutions. S. Azeez Basha (1967) overruled. AMU's own status was left to a regular bench. Justices Surya Kant, Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma dissented.

32.about: The right to move the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights is itself a Fundamental Right. The Court may issue any direction, order or writ (habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto). Ambedkar called it the “heart and soul” of the Constitution. It cannot be suspended except as the Constitution provides (Art. 359).

key.c: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
key.issue: Madras banned the entry of the journal Cross Roads on public-safety grounds. The editor went straight to the Supreme Court.
key.q: Must a petitioner go to the High Court first? Was the ban valid?
key.held: Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, and the Supreme Court is the “protector and guarantor” of FRs; it cannot refuse a petition because a High Court remedy exists. The ban violated 19(1)(a), since “public order” was not then a ground in 19(2).

key.held: Yes. “Appropriate proceedings” in Art. 32 need no fixed form: a letter can be a writ petition, anyone acting in good faith can move for those who cannot, and the Court can appoint commissions to find facts.
key.exam: PIL and epistolary jurisdiction; link to Art. 23 (bonded labour).

key.exam: Basic structure; tribunals and the writ power.

44.about: “The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.” A UCC means one set of civil laws on marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption and succession for all religions. key.c: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum

key.held: Yes, Sec. 125 is secular and applies to all; Mahr is not maintenance. The Court regretted that Art. 44 had remained a dead letter.

key.c: Maru Ram v. Union of India
key.issue: Life convicts challenged Sec. 433A CrPC, which required 14 years of actual jail before release for certain lifers.
key.q: Does Sec. 433A cut down the clemency power, and whose decision is the clemency decision?
key.held: Sec. 433A is valid, but it cannot touch Arts 72 and 161. The power is exercised on the advice of the Union (or State) government, not personally by the President, and courts can review a decision that is arbitrary, mala fide or based on irrelevant grounds.
key.exam: Clemency = government's decision in the President's name.

key.c: Kehar Singh v. Union of India
key.issue: A convict in the Indira Gandhi assassination case asked for an oral hearing before the President decided his mercy petition.

239AA.about: Inserted by the 69th Amendment (1991): Delhi becomes the National Capital Territory with an elected Assembly (70 seats), a Council of Ministers (up to 10%) and a Lieutenant Governor. The Assembly can make laws on State and Concurrent List matters except public order, police and land.

254.about: On a Concurrent List matter, if a State law is repugnant to a law of Parliament, the Union law prevails, whether it was made before or after, and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy. A State law that was reserved for the President and got his assent prevails in that State, until Parliament changes it.

State law on a Concurrent matter, reserved for and assented to by the President, prevails in that State

Parliament can later add to, amend, vary or repeal that State law

key.c: Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay
key.issue: A Bombay Act raised the punishment for breaking food-grain orders; a later Central Act (1950) on the Essential Supplies Act fixed a lower one.
key.q: Does a later Central law on the same subject override the State law under the proviso to 254(2)?
key.held: Yes. Both laws dealt with the same matter (punishment for breaking such orders), so the later Parliament law prevailed over the State's enhanced punishment.
key.exam: Classic proviso case: Parliament can undo a State law even after Presidential assent.

key.c: Deep Chand v. State of UP
key.issue: A UP law nationalising bus routes clashed with a later Central amendment to the Motor Vehicles Act.
key.q: How do we know when two laws are repugnant?
key.held: Laid down three tests: (1) direct conflict between the provisions; (2) Parliament meant to make an exhaustive code; (3) both laws occupy the same field.
key.exam: The three tests are quoted in every later repugnancy case.

key.c: M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India
key.issue: Former TN Chief Minister said the TN Public Men (Criminal Misconduct) Act, 1973 was repugnant to the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act.
key.q: Is a State law repugnant just because it overlaps with Central laws?
key.held: No. Repugnancy needs an irreconcilable conflict; the State Act could stand with the Central laws. Prosecution continued; a Chief Minister is a public servant.
key.exam: Restates the tests: overlap is not enough; there must be a real clash.

key.c: Kaiser-I-Hind v. National Textile Corporation
key.issue: Occupants relied on the Bombay Rents Act (which had Presidential assent) against eviction under the Central Public Premises Act, 1971.
key.q: Does Presidential assent under 254(2) protect a State law against every Central law?
key.held: No. Assent protects the State law only against the Central laws named in the State's proposal. The Public Premises Act prevailed.
key.exam: Presidential assent is limited to its purpose; States must spell out the repugnancy.

key.c: Forum for People's Collective Efforts v. State of West Bengal
key.issue: West Bengal made its own housing law (WB-HIRA, 2017) almost copying the Central RERA, 2016, without Presidential assent.
key.q: Can a State make a parallel law on the same Concurrent subject as a Central law?
key.held: No. WB-HIRA was struck down as repugnant to RERA (Art. 254(1)). The Court restated the three tests and said a State cannot enact a law that covers the same field and creates a parallel regime.
key.exam: Recent example of 254(1); home-buyers get one uniform regime.

minor.c: Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of UP
minor.pt: doctrine of occupied field: no repugnancy unless Parliament has actually covered the field

minor.c: T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe
minor.pt: later Central amendment (1976) to the Food Adulteration Act prevailed over West Bengal's harsher amendment; accused got the lighter punishment

minor.c: State of Maharashtra v. Bharat Shanti Lal Shah
minor.pt: State law (MCOCA) on the same subject held not repugnant; threshold for repugnancy kept high

minor.c: Innoventive Industries v. ICICI Bank
minor.pt: Maharashtra Relief Undertakings Act repugnant to the later IBC, 2016; IBC prevails (254(1))

key.c: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
key.issue: The 1st Amendment (Arts 31A, 31B) cut down the right to property to save land reform laws.
key.q: Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights under Art. 368?
key.held: Yes. 'Law' in Art. 13(2) means ordinary law, not a constitutional amendment, so any part, FRs included, can be amended.
key.exam: Start of the chain (with Sajjan Singh, 1965).

key.c: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
key.issue: Punjab land-ceiling laws and the 1st, 4th and 17th Amendments were challenged.
key.q: Is an amendment 'law' under Art. 13, so that it cannot abridge FRs?
key.held: Yes: an amendment is 'law'; Parliament cannot take away or abridge FRs. Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh overruled, but applied only for the future (prospective overruling), so past amendments survived.
key.exam: Provoked the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments.

key.c: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
key.issue: The head of the Edneer Mutt challenged Kerala land reform laws and the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments.
key.q: Is Parliament's amending power unlimited?
key.held: Parliament can amend any part, including FRs, but cannot destroy the basic structure. Golaknath overruled; 24th Am upheld; the part of Art 31C barring judicial review (25th Am) struck down. Cut-off date: 24 April 1973.
key.exam: The anchor case: largest bench ever.

key.c: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
key.issue: The 39th Amendment (Art 329A) put the election of the PM and Speaker beyond courts while her appeal against the Allahabad HC verdict was pending.
key.q: Can an amendment validate a disputed election by excluding judicial review?
key.held: Art 329A(4) struck down: free and fair elections, rule of law and judicial review are basic features.
key.exam: First use of basic structure to strike an amendment.

key.c: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
key.issue: Challenge to the 42nd Amendment's Art 368(4)-(5) and the widened Art 31C.
key.q: Can Parliament make its amending power unlimited and unreviewable?
key.held: No. Cl (4) and (5) struck down: limited amending power, judicial review and the FR-DPSP balance are basic structure; the 42nd Am's extension of 31C to all DPSPs struck down. Justice P.N. Bhagwati partly dissented (on 31C).
key.exam: 'Parliament cannot convert a limited power into an unlimited one' (Mains 2019 theme).

key.c: Waman Rao v. Union of India
key.issue: Maharashtra land-ceiling laws placed in the Ninth Schedule were challenged.
key.q: From when does the basic structure test apply?
key.held: To amendments made after 24 April 1973; earlier Ninth Schedule entries stay valid.
key.exam: The cut-off rule Coelho built on.

key.c: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
key.issue: Laws that courts had struck down and that were then put in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 (a Tamil Nadu land law among them) claimed immunity under Art 31B.
key.q: Does a Ninth Schedule entry give blanket immunity?
key.held: No. Laws added after 24 April 1973 can be tested against the basic structure, especially the essence of Arts 14, 19 and 21 (rights test, essence of right test).
key.exam: Judicial review as a key basic feature.

key.c: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC case)

key.q: Does the NJAC violate judicial independence?
key.held: 99th Amendment struck down: independence of the judiciary (judicial primacy in appointments) is basic structure; collegium revived. Justice J. Chelameswar dissented.
key.exam: Recent use of basic structure against an amendment.

In August 2019 CO 272 applied the whole Constitution and CO 273 made Art 370's clauses inoperative; the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 created two UTs from 31 October 2019. The Supreme Court upheld this on 11 December 2023.

key.c: In re Article 370 of the Constitution
key.issue: Petitions challenged CO 272, CO 273 and the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019, all made while the State was under President's Rule.
key.q: Could the President end Art 370 after the J&K Constituent Assembly had dissolved, without the State's concurrence, and could the State be split into UTs?
key.held: Upheld. J&K kept no internal sovereignty after accession; Art 370 was a temporary, transitional provision (asymmetric federalism). The 370(3) power survived the Constituent Assembly's dissolution; State concurrence was not needed to apply the whole Constitution. But amending Art 370 through Art 367 (CO 272) was invalid, 'amendment through the back door'; this did not change the result. Ladakh UT upheld under Art 3; J&K's change to a UT left open on the Union's promise to restore statehood; Assembly polls ordered by 30 September 2024. Justice S.K. Kaul suggested a truth and reconciliation commission.
key.exam: Asymmetric federalism; whether a State can be made a UT is still open; Assembly polls were held in Sept-Oct 2024.
